market: sleep improvement apps, English (FICTIONAL sample market)
notice: FICTIONAL example: the market, the ads and the team are invented. The snapshot numbers are real Jev output on the invented ads. Budget and CPA are example values.

constraints.product: Brand Z (fictional): a sleep routine app with an 8-minute guided wind-down (lights, breathing, a short story).
constraints.brand_rules: Calm, plain tone. No medical claims: never cure, treat, fix or diagnose insomnia or any condition. No invented reviews or user counts. No before and after of bodies or faces.
constraints.offers: 7-day free trial, then an annual plan; the annual price is shown in full wherever a price appears.
constraints.can_produce: Static: one in-house designer. Motion: one motion designer for screen-based and kinetic type work. UGC: one creator shoot per month.

decisions.rationale: No static in the market sets the routine against an alternative, while 8 of 12 lead with an outcome promise and all 5 advertisers use it. A comparison hook stands apart in the feed without needing a stronger promise than the others.
decisions.hypothesis: A comparison headline (routine against an alternative) gets a lower cost per trial than an outcome-promise control, because nobody else in the feed uses it.

decisions.rationale: Outcome promises are the crowded default, so one concept enters it with a sharper line: hook specificity averages 1.25 on a 0 to 3 scale and no static reaches the top level (audience, promise and a timeframe). The promise is about the routine, which the product can keep, not about sleep results.
decisions.hypothesis: An outcome promise with audience, promise and timeframe in one line beats the market's vaguer promises on cost per trial.

decisions.rationale: Health and guaranteed-result claims are common in this market (2 statics flagged, 5 more in review). Brand rules forbid them and they invite rejection. No concept uses cure, fix or a sleep-time guarantee.

9 of 12 videos carry the hook with a spoken line and none with a visual action; none shows the product in the first 3 seconds (one in review). Two concepts open on the product doing something on screen, with no talking.
decisions.hypothesis: Opening on the product doing something, with no speech in seconds 0 to 3, holds more viewers past 3 seconds than a spoken opening.

decisions.rationale: Talking heads are half of the market and every advertiser runs one, so the team's monthly UGC shoot only earns its place with a different opening: the app on screen in the creator's hand from the first frame and a specific line (video hook specificity averages 1.36 of 3). Pacing stays near the market median of 1.58 cuts per 10 seconds; the difference is in the first 3 seconds, not the edit.
decisions.hypothesis: A talking head with the app in hand from the first frame beats a talking head that shows the app later, on cost per trial.

decisions.rationale: 4 videos are flagged for health or result claims and 4 more sit in review, including a 'completely cured' line. No script promises a cure, a number of hours or minutes to fall asleep, or a fixed relationship or work outcome.

motion_briefs.concept: One tap and the room goes dark
motion_briefs.format: screen-led motion: phone screen footage composited with a real bedroom, no presenter
motion_briefs.voice_or_captions: No voice-over in seconds 0 to 3. Calm voice-over from second 3. Captions burned in for every spoken line, white on a soft dark band inside the 9:16 safe zone.
motion_briefs.pacing_sound: Market median is 1.58 cuts per 10 s and 5 s per shot; keep the opening a single continuous shot so the action carries the hook, then cut every 3 to 4 s. Sound: a soft tap at 0.5 s, room tone drops when the light goes off, quiet piano from second 3.
